blocks.heading: Longshore drift
blocks.text: Longshore drift is the net transport of beach material along the coast through oblique swash and returning backwash. When breaking waves approach the shore obliquely, swash runs diagonally up the beach. Gravity then returns backwash more directly downslope. Repeated movements give sediment a zigzag path with a net alongshore component. The direction depends on wave approach and the orientation of the shore; it is not invariably north, south or to the right of a page. Local wind can influence wave direction, but distant swell and refraction mean drift cannot always be inferred from the local wind. A labelled diagram shows the prevailing wind, the oblique swash, the backwash running straight down the beach and an arrow for the direction of drift. Longshore currents can also transport sediment within the nearshore system.

blocks.text:
In an original plan, sea lies west of a north–south beach. Swash carries a marked grain northeastward and backwash returns it roughly westward. After repeated cycles its position is farther north, supporting northward net drift for that interval. If the approach direction reverses later, transport can change. The observed short-term direction does not prove a single direction throughout the year. A clear diagram needs a north arrow, land and sea positions, wave approach and separate water or sediment arrows.

![Zigzag path of a grain giving northward net drift](../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-029-INTERP-answer.png)

blocks.text: A groyne crossing the beach can intercept part of this sediment movement, producing greater accumulation on the updrift side under suitable conditions. That pattern can help infer the dominant drift during the observed period, provided sediment supply and other controls are considered. Do not identify direction from a groyne alone without the beach-level or movement evidence. This connects longshore drift to spits, beaches and coastal management, where reducing supply past one structure can affect a neighbouring reach. Material trapped locally is part of a wider sediment system, not sand created by the structure itself.
